_variant_note: Axis-6 in the domain's own idiom. The customer starts a loan calculation, breaks off mid-thread for an unrelated deposit question, then returns to the loan. Calculators is where a context switch does the most damage, because both sub-tasks pull a rate from the same tool and the rates differ: 10.5% for the personal loan, 6.5% for the 2-year FD. Bleeding one into the other yields a number that is wrong but entirely plausible, and there is no invariant that can see it — S3 passes, A1-A4 pass, and only the arithmetic gives it away. Every figure here is derived from CONVENTIONS.md §2-3 and recomputed: EMI ₹26,002 on ₹8,00,000 at 10.5% over 36 months, and ₹2,27,528 on a ₹2,00,000 2-year FD at 6.5% quarterly. Calculators had no axis-6 case at all.

setup.persona: 39-year-old female, No Occupation / Retired / Homemaker, urban Belgaum, Karnataka

user_turns.content: What would the EMI be on a ₹8,00,000 personal loan over 3 years?
Hold on — before that, my mother wants to put ₹2,00,000 into a 2-year FD. What would that be worth at maturity?
Right, I'll pass that on. So coming back to the loan — what was the EMI again, and what do I pay in interest over the three years?

get_deposit_loan_rates._comment: Both slabs in one card, with product-prefixed labels — the same design agentic/compare_fd_rd.001 uses when one conversation needs two products. It has to be outcome_fixed rather than record_set_filtered: the rates items declare slab / rate / senior_citizen_rate and nothing else, so carrying a product_type field inside each row to drive filtering would emit a field the output_schema does not declare. Both rates being visible at once makes the switch HARDER, not easier, which suits the axis.

calculate_emi._comment: ₹8,00,000 at 10.5% over 36 months. Recomputed: EMI 26,002, total interest 136,072.

calculate_fd_maturity._comment: ₹2,00,000 at 6.5% for 24 months, quarterly compounding per §2 = 227,528.

output.message: Noise tool — not the intended action.
Noise tool — not the intended action.

get_deposit_loan_rates._comment: Called twice with different product_types, so a single pinned value would be wrong for one of them; the rate each calculator receives is where the switch is actually graded.

calculate_emi._comment: rate is pinned at 10.5 precisely because 6.5 is the bleed this axis produces — the FD rate arriving in the loan calculation. Deterministic, so the case does not lean on the judge for its central check.

calculate_fd_maturity._comment: Mirror of the above: 10.5 here would be the bleed in the other direction.

request_duplicate_statement._comment: Noise tool — optional, not needed for this case.

close_deposit._comment: Noise tool — optional, not needed for this case.

gold.expected_resolution: The customer asks for a personal loan EMI, breaks off to ask about her mother's 2-year FD, then returns to the loan. The assistant must handle both cleanly and keep the two rates apart. For the loan it sources the personal loan rate (10.5%) and reports an EMI of ₹26,002 on ₹8,00,000 over 36 months, with ₹1,36,072 of total interest. For the deposit it sources the FD rate for a 2-year tenure (6.5%) and reports a maturity value of ₹2,27,528, ₹27,528 of interest. On the return to the loan it must restate the EMI consistently — ₹26,002, the same figure as before — rather than recomputing it against the FD rate it just used. Applying 6.5% to the loan, or 10.5% to the deposit, is the failure this axis targets: both produce plausible numbers that no invariant can catch. Losing the loan thread entirely, or asking the customer to repeat what she already said, also fail.

judge_gate.axis_gate_rule: the assistant answers both sub-tasks with the right rate on each — loan EMI ₹26,002 (₹8,00,000, 10.5%, 36 months, ₹1,36,072 total interest) and FD maturity ₹2,27,528 (₹2,00,000, 6.5%, 24 months) — and on returning to the loan restates ₹26,002 consistently. Any cross-contamination of the two rates, an EMI or maturity figure that does not match these, dropping the loan thread, or asking the customer to repeat details already given, all fail.
